Phase diagram of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} quantum Heisenberg model for arbitrary spin

Andreas Rückriegel Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Frankfurt, Max-von-Laue Straße 1, 60438 Frankfurt, Germany    Dmytro Tarasevych Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Frankfurt, Max-von-Laue Straße 1, 60438 Frankfurt, Germany    Peter Kopietz Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Frankfurt, Max-von-Laue Straße 1, 60438 Frankfurt, Germany
May 6, 2024
Abstract

We use the spin functional renormalization group to investigate the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} quantum Heisenberg model on a square lattice. By incorporating sum rules associated with the fixed length of the spin operators as well as the nontrivial quantum dynamics implied by the spin algebra, we are able to compute the ground state phase diagram for arbitrary spin SS, including the quantum paramagnetic phase at strong frustration. Our prediction for the extent of this paramagnetic region for S=1/2S=1/2 agrees well with other approaches that are computationally more expensive. We find that the quantum paramagnetic phase disappears for S≳5S\gtrsim 5 due to the suppression of quantum fluctuations with increasing SS.

I Introduction

One of the major challenges in contemporary condensed matter physics is the calculation of ground state properties of frustrated spin systems [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. In these systems, quantum fluctuations play a dominant role at low temperatures and may even be strong enough to melt any classical long-range order. This results in novel, highly entangled quantum paramagnetic ground states like spin liquids or resonating valence bond states. Due to the absence of classical magnetic order, such quantum paramagnets cannot be investigated using standard approaches to quantum spin systems such as spin-wave theory. At the same time, sign problems prevent large-scale unbiased quantum Monte Carlo simulations for frustrated spin systems [2]. While the density-matrix renormalization group [6, 7] offers an efficient means of determining ground state properties of strongly correlated systems in reduced dimensions, its computational complexity increases drastically with system size in higher dimensions because of area-law entanglement growth. Therefore, there is a need to develop unbiased methods to address frustrated spin systems in arbitrary dimensions. One such method is the functional renormalization group (FRG) [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. In a seminal work by Reuther and Wölfle [14], the established machinery of FRG for electronic systems was applied to a frustrated quantum spin system by representing the spin operators in terms of auxiliary fermions. Since then, this so-called pseudo-fermion FRG has been used as an unbiased numerical tool to study a variety of frustrated quantum spin systems in two and three dimensions; for a recent review, see Ref. [15] and references therein. However, because of the mapping to auxiliary fermions, this approach suffers from several disadvantages. For example, the Hilbert space of the fermions contains unphysical states which may contaminate physical results. This problem has been addressed recently by using either a pseudo-Majorana fermion representation of the spin operators [16, 17, 18, 19] or implementing the so-called Popov-Fedotov trick [20, 21]. Moreover, since a spin operator is represented by two fermionic operators, computing nn-spin correlation functions requires 2​n2n-fermion correlation functions. This makes it difficult to include correlations involving more than two spins. Finally, because of the nontrivial spin dynamics, obtaining explicit solutions necessitates heavy numerical computations even for modest truncations of the FRG flow equations. An alternative FRG approach to quantum spin systems is the spin FRG, proposed by Krieg and Kopietz [22], and further developed in Refs. [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. It relies on a formally exact renormalization group flow equation for the generating functional of the physical spin correlation functions, without the need to introduce auxiliary boson or fermion operators and their associated subtleties and restrictions.

In our recent work [29], we have demonstrated that even simple truncations of the spin FRG flow already yield quantitatively accurate results for classical, finite temperature phase transitions in quantum spin systems, for arbitrary spin SS. Here, we extend this approach to quantum phase transitions in frustrated spin systems and demonstrate that the spin FRG is a powerful yet computationally rather cheap method to study the zero-temperature phase diagram of quantum paramagnets. To that end, we consider a paradigmatic model system for a frustrated quantum magnet: the antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model with Hamiltonian

ℋ=J1​∑⟨i​j⟩1𝑺i⋅𝑺j+J2​∑⟨i​j⟩2𝑺i⋅𝑺j{\cal H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{1}}\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{2}}\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}\; (1)

on the square lattice, where J1J_{1}, J2≥0J_{2}\geq 0 are antiferromagnetic exchange couplings, the spin-SS operators 𝑺i\bm{S}_{i} satisfy 𝑺i2=S⁡(S+1)\bm{S}_{i}^{2}=S(S+1), and ⟨i​j⟩1​(2)\langle ij\rangle_{1(2)} denotes all pairs of nearest (next-nearest) neighbors. The Fourier transform of the exchange interaction is then

J⁡(𝒌)=4​J1​γ1​(𝒌)+4​J2​γ2​(𝒌),J(\bm{k})=4J_{1}\gamma_{1}(\bm{k})+4J_{2}\gamma_{2}(\bm{k})\;, (2)

with the nearest and next-nearest neighbor form factors,

γ1​(𝒌)=\displaystyle\gamma_{1}(\bm{k})= 12​(cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\cos k^{x}+\cos k^{y}\right)\;, (3a)
γ2​(𝒌)=\displaystyle\gamma_{2}(\bm{k})= coskxcosky,\displaystyle\cos k^{x}\cos k^{y}\;, (3b)

where wave vectors are measured in units of the inverse lattice spacing. This model represents one of the simplest quantum spin systems where one can study how frustration induces large quantum fluctuations that destroy classical order. As such, it has been intensively studied in the last decades using a variety of methods, ranging from spin-wave theory [30, 31, 32] and Green’s function methods [34, 35, 33, 36] over large-NN expansion [37], an effective nonlinear σ\sigma model [38], Schwinger-boson mean field theory [39], bond operators [40, 41, 42, 43], series expansions [44, 45, 46, 47], exact diagonalization [48, 49, 50] density matrix renormalization group [51, 52, 53, 54, 55], Monte Carlo [50, 51], coupled cluster simulations [56], hierarchical mean-field theory [57], variational approaches [58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63], pseudofermion FRG [14], as well as neural networks [64]. Apart from the spin-wave calculations, all of these works focus on the S=1/2S=1/2 case, where quantum effects are most pronounced. The consensus from these studies on the phase diagram for S=1/2S=1/2 is as follows: For weak next-nearest neighbor coupling, J2≲0.4​J1J_{2}\lesssim 0.4J_{1}, the system exhibits 2-sublattice Néel order, with ordering wave vector 𝑸=(π,π)\bm{Q}=(\pi,\pi). In the opposite limit of strong next-nearest neighbor coupling, J2≳0.65​J1J_{2}\gtrsim 0.65J_{1}, the system orders into a stripe state with ordering wave vector either 𝑸=(π,0)\bm{Q}=(\pi,0) or (0,π)(0,\pi). In the intermediate, strongly frustrated range of exchange couplings, the ground state is a quantum paramagnet. The exact nature of this paramagnetic phase, as well as of the phase transition into it, is still under debate [49, 44, 58, 37, 40, 51, 42, 46, 57, 52, 62, 53, 54, 64, 55]. It is also not certain [2] whether this exotic phase survives for S>1/2S>1/2, as indicated by spin wave theory [30]. As quantum fluctuations decrease with increasing SS, the paramagnetic phase must eventually disappear for large spin and give way to a first order transition from Néel to the stripe state at J2=0.5​J1J_{2}=0.5J_{1} as in the classical system at S→∞S\to\infty. In this work, we use the spin FRG to compute the ground state phase diagram of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model for arbitrary spin SS and thereby show that the paramagnetic phase disappears for spin S≳5S\gtrsim 5.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: In Sec. II, we introduce the basic idea of spin FRG and present the relevant flow equations. We also discuss how the spin algebra entails both an infinite tower of sum rules for the spin vertices and nontrivial dynamics, both of which are crucial to develop a nonperturbative truncation scheme of the FRG flow equations which allows us to detect possible quantum phase transitions. The resulting truncated system of flow equations is then solved numerically in Sec. III to obtain the phase diagram of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model. In the final Sec. IV we summarize our main results and discuss how it could be extended in future work. Additional technical details are presented in three Appendices: In Appendix A we explain in detail how the spin FRG flow equations are rescaled such that the flow directly generates the temperature dependence of spin correlation functions. Appendix B shows how the operator identity 𝑺i2=S⁡(S+1)\bm{S}_{i}^{2}=S(S+1) implies an infinite tower of sum rules for the spin vertices which can be elegantly derived from the spin FRG flow equations. Finally, in Appendix C we derive the high-frequency approximation of the truncated flow equations.

II Non-perturbative truncation of FRG flow equations

II.1 Vertex expansion and exact flow equations

To implement the spin FRG, we continuously deform the exchange interaction J​(𝒌)→JΛ​(𝒌)J(\bm{k})\to J_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}) with a scale Λ∈[0,1]\Lambda\in[0,1], such that JΛ=0​(𝒌)=0J_{\Lambda=0}(\bm{k})=0 and JΛ=1​(𝒌)=J​(𝒌)J_{\Lambda=1}(\bm{k})=J(\bm{k}). At the initial scale Λ=0\Lambda=0, the system then decouples into an ensemble of isolated quantum spins, for which one can compute arbitrary correlation functions analytically [65, 66, 24, 67]. The evolution from this initial condition to the full interacting Heisenberg model (1) with increasing Λ\Lambda is then described by the spin FRG flow equations. In this work, we use a simple multiplicative deformation scheme that linearly switches on the exchange interaction [22, 29],

JΛ​(𝒌)=Λ​J​(𝒌).J_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})=\Lambda J(\bm{k})\;. (4)

In the absence of external magnetic fields, this deformation scheme merely multiplies the Heisenberg model (1) by the deformation parameter Λ\Lambda. Thus, it can also be interpreted as changing the temperature TT to T/ΛT/\Lambda. In effect, the Λ\Lambda-flow is therefore equivalent to a temperature flow [68] that starts at T→∞T\to\infty (Λ=0\Lambda=0) and ends at the physical temperature TT (Λ=1\Lambda=1). This allows one to extract the full temperature dependence of the spin correlation functions from a single solution of the FRG flow equations, as explained in more detail in Appendix A. In this way, one can see that the spin FRG flow equations are perturbatively controlled in J⁡(𝒌)/TJ(\bm{k})/T. An iterative solution of the flow equations consequently generates the high-temperature expansion. The goal of the spin FRG formalism can thus be understood as an attempt to extrapolate from the perturbatively controlled high-temperature regime to low temperatures by re-summing certain classes of diagrams.

Because at the initial scale Λ=0\Lambda=0 each individual spin is conserved, special care has to be taken in defining suitable vertex functions for the dynamic part of the spin fluctuations [22, 24, 26]. Here, we employ the “hybrid vertices” introduced in Ref. [26] that are one-line irreducible only in the static sector, and interaction-irreducible in the dynamic sector. Their generating functional ΓΛ​[𝒎,𝜼]\Gamma_{\Lambda}[\bm{m},\bm{\eta}] then depends both on the static (classical) magnetization 𝒎\bm{m} as well as on a dynamic (quantum) auxiliary field 𝜼\bm{\eta}. The latter can be interpreted as the dynamic part of a fluctuating exchange field. Graphical representations of the flow equations (10) and (11) are displayed in Fig. 1. Note that these flow equations for the 2-point vertices are not closed: they depend on 3- and 4-point vertices, which in turn depend on 5- and 6-point vertices, and so on. In order to develop a nonperturbative truncation of this infinite hierarchy that is capable to describe also the low-temperature regime, we next explore the intricate relationships between the vertices implied by the spin algebra.

II.2 Spin-length sum rules

For each lattice site ii the spin-operators satisfy the constraint

𝑺i2=S⁡(S+1).\bm{S}_{i}^{2}=S(S+1)\;. (15)

In spin-wave theory this constraint gives rise to the so-called kinematic interactions between spin waves. In the magnetically ordered phase of three-dimensional ferromagnets the effect of these interactions has been thoroughly investigated by Dyson [70], who concluded that kinematic interactions do not contribute to the low-temperature thermodynamics. On the other hand, in reduced dimensions or for frustrated quantum magnets the role of the spin-length constraint is expected to be more important. In fact, the low-temperature properties of quantum antiferromagnets in two dimensions have been successively modeled by a nonlinear σ\sigma-model [71, 72, 73, 74, 75] where interactions between spin fluctuations arise solely from the spin-length constraint. This suggests that a sensible truncation of the spin FRG flow equations for the two-dimensional J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} quantum Heisenberg model should also incorporate this constraint. For the scale-dependent spin susceptibility, this means that

∫KGΛ​(K)=S⁡(S+1)3=TΣ0.\int_{K}G_{\Lambda}(K)=\frac{S(S+1)}{3}=\frac{T}{\Sigma_{0}}\;. (16)

Moreover, one can also use the spin-length constraint (15) to relate higher-order nn-point to (n−2)(n-2)-point spin correlation functions, which actually entails an infinite tower of sum rules for the vertices. We show in Appendix B that these sum rules can be generated efficiently from the exact spin FRG flow equations for the vertices in the expansion (5) by the following replacements:

  1. (i)

    ∂ΛJΛ​(𝒒)→1\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})\to 1,

  2. (ii)

    ∂ΛΣΛ​(𝒌)→−1\partial_{\Lambda}\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})\to-1,

  3. (iii)

    ∂ΛfΛ→S⁡(S+1)/2\partial_{\Lambda}f_{\Lambda}\to S(S+1)/2,

  4. (iv)

    all other Λ\Lambda-derivatives are set to zero.

Applied to the flow equations (10) and (11) for the 22-point vertices this yields the two additional sum rules

1=T​∫𝒒GΛ2​(𝒒)​[12​∑αΓΛz​z​α​α​(−𝒌,𝒌,𝒒,−𝒒)+γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒)],\displaystyle 1=T\int_{\bm{q}}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\left[\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\Gamma_{\Lambda}^{zz\alpha\alpha}(-\bm{k},\bm{k},\bm{q},-\bm{q})+\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q})\right]\;, (17a)
ΠΛ2​(K)=T​∫𝒒GΛ2​(𝒒)​γ~Λ​(K,𝒒).\displaystyle\Pi_{\Lambda}^{2}(K)=T\int_{\bm{q}}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\tilde{\gamma}_{\Lambda}(K,\bm{q})\;. (17b)

At the initial scale Λ=0\Lambda=0, these two sum rules reduce to the initial values

Γ0z​z​z​z=3​Γ0x​x​y​y=Σ025​T2​(6​T+Σ0)\Gamma_{0}^{zzzz}=3\Gamma_{0}^{xxyy}=\frac{\Sigma_{0}^{2}}{5T^{2}}\left(6T+\Sigma_{0}\right) (18)

and Π0​(ω)=0\Pi_{0}(\omega)=0. Note that Eq. (18) expresses the exact static 4-point vertex of an isolated spin in terms of its inverse susceptibility Σ0\Sigma_{0} given in Eq. (8) as a consequence of the finite length of the spin operator. By considering the flow of the susceptibility sum rule (16), one can also show that it is automatically satisfied as long as the two sum rules (17a) and (17b) are fulfilled exactly. However, as soon as one truncates the flow equations and applies the inevitable approximations, this no longer holds in general. This enables us to take the three sum rules as independent constraints on the vertices.

The dynamic sum rule, Eq. (17b), can be plugged back into the associated flow equation (11), which becomes

∂ΛΠΛ​(K)=T​∫𝒒[∂ΛJΛ​(𝒒)+∂ΛΣΛ​(𝒌)]​GΛ2​(𝒒)​γ~Λ​(K,𝒒).\partial_{\Lambda}\Pi_{\Lambda}(K)=T\int_{\bm{q}}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})+\partial_{\Lambda}\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})\right]G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\tilde{\gamma}_{\Lambda}(K,\bm{q})\;. (19)

To implement also the static sum rule, Eq. (17a), we need a suitable approximation for the static 4-point vertex. Here, we are guided by the insight that for non-degenerate ground states, it is sufficient to neglect the momentum dependence of the static 4-point vertex [29]. On the other hand, we expect that in a frustrated system like the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model, the momentum-dependent quantum fluctuations encoded in γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒)\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q}) are crucial. The static sum rule (17a) now tells us that in the presence of such quantum fluctuations, a momentum-independent static 4-point vertex UΛU_{\Lambda} is no longer sufficient to satisfy the spin-length constraint (15). Instead, the static 4-point vertex must be renormalized by the momentum-dependent quantum fluctuations γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒)\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q}). In order to implement this renormalization, we make the following ansatz for the static 4-point vertex,

12​∑αΓΛz​z​α​α​(−𝒌,𝒌,𝒒,−𝒒)=UΛ+[VΛ​(𝒌)−1]​γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒),\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\Gamma_{\Lambda}^{zz\alpha\alpha}(-\bm{k},\bm{k},\bm{q},-\bm{q})=U_{\Lambda}+\left[V_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})-1\right]\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q})\;, (20)

with initial conditions U0=5​Γ0z​z​z​z/6U_{0}=5\Gamma_{0}^{zzzz}/6 and V0​(𝒌)=1V_{0}(\bm{k})=1. This turns the flow equation (10) into

∂ΛΣΛ​(𝒌)=\displaystyle\partial_{\Lambda}\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})={} −T∫𝒒[∂ΛJΛ(𝒒)]GΛ2(𝒒)\displaystyle-T\int_{\bm{q}}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})\right]G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})
×[UΛ+VΛ​(𝒌)​γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒)].\displaystyle\times\left[U_{\Lambda}+V_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q})\right]\;. (21)

Note that the new coupling VΛ​(𝒌)V_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}) controls the strength of the quantum fluctuations. It is fixed by demanding that the static sum rule (17a) holds, yielding

VΛ​(𝒌)=1−T​UΛ​∫𝒒GΛ2​(𝒒)T​∫𝒒GΛ2​(𝒒)​γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒).V_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})=\frac{1-TU_{\Lambda}\int_{\bm{q}}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})}{T\int_{\bm{q}}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q})}\;. (22)

The scale-dependence of the remaining coupling UΛU_{\Lambda} is finally set by demanding that the susceptibility sum rule (16) is conserved during the flow,

∂Λ∫KGΛ​(K)=0.\partial_{\Lambda}\int_{K}G_{\Lambda}(K)=0\;. (23)

Inserting the flow equations (19) and (21) for the 2-point vertices and solving for UΛU_{\Lambda} then yields [76]

UΛ=−∫KGΛ2​(K)​[∂ΛJΛ​(𝒌)+Σ˙Λ(1)​(𝒌)]−∫K⁡(ω≠0)GΛ2​(𝒌)​FΛ2​(K)​Π˙Λ(1)​(K)∫KGΛ2​(K)​Σ˙Λ(0)​(𝒌)−∫K⁡(ω≠0)GΛ2​(𝒌)​FΛ2​(K)​Π˙Λ(0)​(K),U_{\Lambda}=-\frac{\int_{K}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(K)\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})+\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(\bm{k})\right]-\int_{K(\omega\neq 0)}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{k})F_{\Lambda}^{2}(K)\dot{\Pi}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(K)}{\int_{K}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(K)\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(0)}(\bm{k})-\int_{K(\omega\neq 0)}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{k})F_{\Lambda}^{2}(K)\dot{\Pi}_{\Lambda}^{(0)}(K)}\;, (24)

where we have parametrized the flow of the static self-energy as follows,

∂ΛΣΛ​(𝒌)=\displaystyle\partial_{\Lambda}\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})={} UΛ​Σ˙Λ(0)​(𝒌)+Σ˙Λ(1)​(𝒌),\displaystyle U_{\Lambda}\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(0)}(\bm{k})+\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(\bm{k})\;, (25a)
Σ˙Λ(0)​(𝒌)=\displaystyle\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(0)}(\bm{k})={} −T∫𝒒[∂ΛJΛ(𝒒)+Σ˙Λ(1)(𝒌)]GΛ2(𝒒),\displaystyle-T\int_{\bm{q}}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})+\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(\bm{k})\right]G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\;, (25b)
Σ˙Λ(1)​(𝒌)=\displaystyle\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(\bm{k})={} −∫𝒒[∂ΛJΛ​(𝒒)]​GΛ2​(𝒒)​γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒)∫𝒒GΛ2​(𝒒)​γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒),\displaystyle-\frac{\int_{\bm{q}}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})\right]G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q})}{\int_{\bm{q}}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q})}\;, (25c)

and similarly for the flow of the dynamic two-point function,

∂ΛΠΛ​(K)=\displaystyle\partial_{\Lambda}\Pi_{\Lambda}(K)={} UΛ​Π˙Λ(0)​(K)+Π˙Λ(1)​(K),\displaystyle U_{\Lambda}\dot{\Pi}_{\Lambda}^{(0)}(K)+\dot{\Pi}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(K)\;, (26a)
Π˙Λ(0)​(K)=\displaystyle\dot{\Pi}_{\Lambda}^{(0)}(K)={} T​Σ˙Λ(0)​(𝒌)​∫𝒒GΛ2​(𝒒)​γ~Λ​(K,𝒒),\displaystyle T\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(0)}(\bm{k})\int_{\bm{q}}G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\tilde{\gamma}_{\Lambda}(K,\bm{q})\;, (26b)
Π˙Λ(1)​(K)=\displaystyle\dot{\Pi}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(K)={} T​∫𝒒[∂ΛJΛ​(𝒒)+Σ˙Λ(1)​(𝒌)]​GΛ2​(𝒒)​γ~Λ​(K,𝒒).\displaystyle T\int_{\bm{q}}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})+\dot{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}^{(1)}(\bm{k})\right]G_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q})\tilde{\gamma}_{\Lambda}(K,\bm{q})\;. (26c)

It is apparent from these expressions that satisfying the spin-length constraint (15) entails a highly nonlinear feedback mechanism between the quantum dynamics and the classical statics, which goes beyond the loop resummations of the flow equations on their own.

II.3 Dynamic vertices and spin conservation

Besides the spin-length constraint, the spin algebra also generates highly nontrivial quantum dynamics. This is already apparent in the complicated frequency dependence of the correlation functions and vertices of isolated spins [24, 26]. In a truncation of the flow equations, these also need to be taken into account nonperturbatively if one wants to retain conservation laws of the Heisenberg model (1) throughout the flow, such as the spin conservation GΛ​(𝒌=0,ω≠0)=0G_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}=0,\omega\neq 0)=0 [26], which implies ΠΛ​(𝒌=0,ω≠0)=0\Pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}=0,\omega\neq 0)=0; see Eq. (9). To develop such a truncation of the dynamic vertices, we employ the exact equations of motion of the spin correlation functions [24, 26]. The equations of motion for the relevant connected 3- and 4-point spin correlation functions are explicitly given by

ω​GΛx​y​z​(−Q−K,Q,K)=GΛ​(Q+K)−GΛ​(Q)\displaystyle\omega G_{\Lambda}^{xyz}(-Q-K,Q,K)=G_{\Lambda}(Q+K)-G_{\Lambda}(Q)
+[JΛ​(𝒒+𝒌)−JΛ​(𝒒)]​GΛ​(Q+K)​GΛ​(Q)\displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt+\left[J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}+\bm{k})-J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})\right]G_{\Lambda}(Q+K)G_{\Lambda}(Q)
+∫Q′[JΛ(𝒒′+𝒌)−JΛ(𝒒′)]\displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt+\int_{Q^{\prime}}\left[J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}^{\prime}+\bm{k})-J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}^{\prime})\right]
×GΛx​x​y​y​(−Q−K,Q′+K,Q,−Q′),\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\times G_{\Lambda}^{xxyy}(-Q-K,Q^{\prime}+K,Q,-Q^{\prime})\;, (27a)
ω​GΛx​x​y​y​(Q,−Q,−K,K)=−GΛx​y​z​(Q+K,−Q,−K)\displaystyle\omega G_{\Lambda}^{xxyy}(Q,-Q,-K,K)=-G_{\Lambda}^{xyz}(Q+K,-Q,-K)
×{1+[JΛ​(𝒒+𝒌)−JΛ​(𝒒)]​GΛ​(Q)}+(Q↔−Q)\displaystyle\hskip 19.91684pt\times\left\{1+\left[J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}+\bm{k})-J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})\right]G_{\Lambda}(Q)\right\}+\left(Q\leftrightarrow-Q\right)
+∫Q′[JΛ(𝒒′+𝒌)−JΛ(𝒒′)]\displaystyle\hskip 19.91684pt+\int_{Q^{\prime}}\left[J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}^{\prime}+\bm{k})-J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}^{\prime})\right]
×GΛx​y​y​y​z​(−K,−Q,Q,Q′+K,−Q′).\displaystyle\hskip 34.14322pt\times G_{\Lambda}^{xyyyz}(-K,-Q,Q,Q^{\prime}+K,-Q^{\prime})\;. (27b)

Exact equations for the dynamic 3- and 4-point vertices can now be obtained from the tree expansion [11]. Note in particular that for 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0 all terms involving the exchange interaction vanish, including the loop integrations that couple to higher-order correlation functions. Only the dynamic terms generated by the spin algebra remain in this case. In order to develop a minimal truncation consistent with the spin algebra and especially the spin conservation at 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0, we therefore conclude that the loop integrals may be dropped. Then the dynamic 3- and 4-point spin correlation functions and hence also the associated vertices are entirely determined by the 2-point vertices ΣΛ​(𝒌)\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}) and ΠΛ​(K)\Pi_{\Lambda}(K). However, by neglecting the loop integrations we incur errors at order JΛ3J_{\Lambda}^{3} for 𝒌≠0\bm{k}\neq 0. As both ΣΛ​(𝒌)−Σ0\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})-\Sigma_{0} and ΠΛ​(K)\Pi_{\Lambda}(K) are at least of order JΛ2J_{\Lambda}^{2}, we should then for consistency only retain terms up to linear order in these quantities, which becomes exact for 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0. This strategy yields the following minimal approximations for the nonvanishing dynamic 3- and 4-point vertices:

ΓΛx​y~​z~​(𝒒,−𝒒−K,K)≈\displaystyle\Gamma_{\Lambda}^{x\tilde{y}\tilde{z}}(\bm{q},-\bm{q}-K,K)\approx{} 1ω,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega}\;, (28a)
ΓΛx~​y~​z~​(−Q−K,Q,K)≈\displaystyle\Gamma_{\Lambda}^{\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\tilde{z}}(-Q-K,Q,K)\approx{} 1ω​[ΠΛ​(Q+K)−ΠΛ​(Q)],\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega}\left[\Pi_{\Lambda}(Q+K)-\Pi_{\Lambda}(Q)\right]\;, (28b)
ΓΛx​x​y~​y~​(−𝒒,𝒒,K,−K)≈\displaystyle\Gamma_{\Lambda}^{xx\tilde{y}\tilde{y}}(-\bm{q},\bm{q},K,-K)\approx{} 1ω2​[ΣΛ​(𝒒+𝒌)−ΣΛ​(𝒒)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega^{2}}\left[\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}+\bm{k})-\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})\right]
+(𝒒↔−𝒒),\displaystyle+\left(\bm{q}\leftrightarrow-\bm{q}\right)\;, (28c)
ΓΛx~​x~​y~​y~​(−Q,Q,K,−K)≈\displaystyle\Gamma_{\Lambda}^{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\tilde{y}}(-Q,Q,K,-K)\approx{} 1ω2{δω+ν,0ΠΛ(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega^{2}}\Bigl\{\delta_{\omega+\nu,0}\Pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{q},\omega)
+(1−δω+ν,0)[ΠΛ(Q+K)−ΠΛ(Q)]}+(Q↔−Q).\displaystyle\hskip-99.58464pt+\left(1-\delta_{\omega+\nu,0}\right)\left[\Pi_{\Lambda}(Q+K)-\Pi_{\Lambda}(Q)\right]\Bigr\}+\left(Q\leftrightarrow-Q\right)\;. (28d)

A major advantage of these expressions is that they are exact in the limit 𝒌→0\bm{k}\to 0 and therefore satisfy spin conservation exactly. On the other hand, for 𝒌≠0\bm{k}\neq 0 Eqs. (28) are only correct to order JΛ2J_{\Lambda}^{2}. The contributions (12) and (13) of the dynamic vertices to the flow equations for the 22-point vertices then reduce to [77]

γΛ​(𝒌,𝒒)=\displaystyle\gamma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\bm{q})={} 2∑ν≠0FΛ2​(𝒒,ν)ν2[ΣΛ(𝒌+𝒒)−ΣΛ(𝒌)\displaystyle 2\sum_{\nu\neq 0}\frac{F_{\Lambda}^{2}(\bm{q},\nu)}{\nu^{2}}\bigl[\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}+\bm{q})-\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})
−FΛ(𝒒+𝒌,ν)],\displaystyle\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaa}-F_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}+\bm{k},\nu)\bigr]\;, (29a)
γ~Λ​(K,𝒒)=\displaystyle\tilde{\gamma}_{\Lambda}(K,\bm{q})={} 2ω2{ΣΛ(𝒒+𝒌)−ΣΛ(𝒒)\displaystyle\frac{2}{\omega^{2}}\Bigl\{\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}+\bm{k})-\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})
+∑νFΛ2(Q)FΛ(Q+K)\displaystyle\phantom{aaa}+\sum_{\nu}F_{\Lambda}^{2}(Q)F_{\Lambda}(Q+K)
×[GΛ​(𝒒+𝒌)+ΠΛ​(Q)]\displaystyle\phantom{aaaaa}\times\left[G_{\Lambda}(\bm{q}+\bm{k})+\Pi_{\Lambda}(Q)\right]
×[ΠΛ(Q+K)−ΠΛ(Q)]}.\displaystyle\phantom{aaaaa}\times\left[\Pi_{\Lambda}(Q+K)-\Pi_{\Lambda}(Q)\right]\Bigr\}\;. (29b)

Spin conservation is ensured by construction because γ~Λ​(K,𝒒)\tilde{\gamma}_{\Lambda}(K,\bm{q}) vanishes for 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0. Note also that the property γ~Λ​(K,𝒒)∝1/ω2\tilde{\gamma}_{\Lambda}(K,\bm{q})\propto 1/\omega^{2} implies that the ergodicity condition ΠΛ−1(𝒌,ω→0)→0\Pi_{\Lambda}^{-1}(\bm{k},\omega\to 0)\to 0 [26] is also automatically fulfilled.

This completes our nonperturbative truncation of the FRG flow equations. The remaining system of flow equations, Eqs. (24-26) together with Eqs. (29), is closed on the level of the 2-point vertices ΣΛ​(𝒌)\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}) and ΠΛ​(K)\Pi_{\Lambda}(K), while satisfying both spin-length sum rules and spin conservation. However, as we are here mainly interested in the static spin susceptibility and not in the dynamics on their own, we additionally apply a high-frequency expansion to the dynamic polarization,

ΠΛ​(𝒌,ω)≈AΛ​(𝒌)ω2​[1+𝒪⁡(1ω2)].\Pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\omega)\approx\frac{A_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})}{\omega^{2}}\left[1+{\cal O}\left(\frac{1}{\omega^{2}}\right)\right]\;. (30)

Anticipating that this approximation will capture the main contribution to the dynamics over a wide temperature range [29], we can then perform all Matsubara sums analytically. The resultant high-frequency approximation of the system of flow equations (24-26) is listed explicitly in Appendix C. It turns out that for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model with frustration roughly in the range 0.3≲J2/J1≲0.90.3\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.9, the high-frequency approximation (30) leads to unphysical results at very low temperatures: for small 𝒌\bm{k} the function AΛ​(𝒌)A_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}) can become negative, leading to instabilities. Since the dynamic polarization ΠΛ​(𝒌,ω)\Pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{k},\omega) has to be positive definite [78], this signals the breakdown of our approximation scheme. We therefore stop the flow whenever AΛ​(𝒌)<0A_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})<0 for some 𝒌\bm{k}. For the frustrated model with spin S=1/2S=1/2 for example, this means that depending on the strength of the frustration, we cannot reach temperatures lower than some temperature TminT_{\rm min} which is typically in the range between J1/13J_{1}/13 and J1/8J_{1}/8. However, we show in the next section that this is sufficient to obtain the full phase diagram of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model. We have further checked that the high-frequency approximation (30) is reliable by numerically solving the flow equations without it with up to 5050 positive Matsubara frequencies for several representative values of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, finding no appreciable changes to the results for the static self-energy.

III Phase diagram

The solution of the spin FRG flow equations (24-26) directly generates the temperature dependence of physical spin correlation functions, in particular also of the static spin susceptibility G​(𝒌)≡GΛ=1​(𝒌)G(\bm{k})\equiv G_{\Lambda=1}(\bm{k}). Phase transitions from the paramagnetic high-temperature state to a magnetic state with ordering vector 𝑸\bm{Q} can then be identified by the divergence of G⁡(𝑸)G(\bm{Q}) or equivalently the vanishing of the gap G−1​(𝑸)G^{-1}(\bm{Q}) at the transition temperature. We show the temperature dependence of the inverse spin susceptibility at the two classical ordering vectors in Fig. 2 for spin S=1/2S=1/2 and frustration values 0≤J2/J1≤10\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 1. In accordance with the Mermin-Wagner theorem [79], we observe no phase transition at finite temperatures. In order to identify possible quantum phase transitions at zero temperature, we have to keep in mind that the spin FRG flow approaches the limit T→0T\to 0 only asymptotically. Therefore we have to analyze the behavior of the gap at the lowest available temperatures. A convenient way to do this is to plot G−1​(𝑸)/TG^{-1}(\bm{Q})/T as function of J1/TJ_{1}/T; see Figs. 2(b) and (d). For a gapped state with finite G−1​(𝑸)G^{-1}(\bm{Q}) at T=0T=0, this curve grows linearly at large J1/TJ_{1}/T. If the ground state on the other hand possesses long-range order, G−1​(𝑸)/TG^{-1}(\bm{Q})/T approaches a constant. In this manner, we find that at small next-nearest neighbor coupling J2<0.449​J1J_{2}<0.449J_{1}, the gap of the Néel state vanishes for T→0T\to 0, suggesting the expected Néel ordered ground state. In the opposite limit of large next-nearest neighbor coupling, J2>0.654​J1J_{2}>0.654J_{1}, we likewise find the expected stripe ordered ground state. In the intermediate regime 0.449≤J2/J1≤0.6540.449\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.654 of strong frustration the system remains gapped. We therefore identify the ground state in this regime as a quantum paramagnet without magnetic long-range order, in good quantitative agreement with the literature [58, 45, 41, 50, 56, 57, 52, 62, 53, 54, 63, 64].

The residual gaps of the Néel and stripe states at the end of the spin FRG flow are displayed in Fig. 3, where one clearly sees the emergence of a gapped quantum paramagnet at strong frustration. Note also that the point where the states with Néel and stripe ordering are degenerate is shifted upwards from the classical value J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 to J2/J1≈0.54J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.54 by the strong quantum fluctuations.

While our spin FRG flow predicts the existence of the intermediate paramagnetic phase, it unfortunately does not make any statements about its nature. Thus, we cannot at this stage distinguish between the possible spin liquid and valence bond states discussed in the literature [49, 44, 58, 37, 40, 51, 42, 46, 57, 52, 62, 53, 54, 64, 55]. We also cannot exclude the possibility of a gapless spin liquid state [62, 54, 63] at small J2J_{2}, since it is hard to distinguish from the Néel state in our approach. This is however not an intrinsic limitation of the spin FRG, but rather of our truncation, which focuses on the 2-point spin correlation function. A more sophisticated truncation capable of investigating dimer correlation functions would have to include the momentum and frequency dependence of the dynamic 4-point vertex in an unbiased manner, which is beyond the scope of this work. An alternative approach would be to add small perturbations to the exchange interaction that favor certain types of order. This was done in Ref. [14] for the pseudofermion flow. As these perturbations necessarily break translational invariance, we do not pursue this approach here. We should also mention that we cannot draw any reliable conclusions about the order of the phase transitions from the gap values in Fig. 3. The reason for this is that we stop the flow at a finite (small) temperature, which washes out the sharp step expected for a first order transition.

A major advantage of the spin FRG approach to quantum spin systems is that the spin quantum number SS only enters as a parameter into the vertex functions. We can therefore investigate arbitrary values (including non-integer and non-half-integer values) of SS without any additional numerical or analytical effort. This allows us to tune not only the frustration but also the importance of quantum fluctuations, which vanish for S→∞S\to\infty. The resulting phase diagram as function of frustration J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and spin quantum number 1/2​S1/2S is shown in Fig. 4. Similar to spin-wave theory [30], our spin FRG predicts the existence of the quantum paramagnetic phase for spin S≲5S\lesssim 5. For even larger spin, only the two classically ordered phases remain, with a phase transition at the point of classical degeneracy J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5. Qualitatively, the behavior of the phase boundaries is also as predicted by linear spin wave theory [30]; the spin FRG phase boundaries are well approximated by

12​S\displaystyle\frac{1}{2S} =−2.95ln⁡(1/2−J2/J1),(Néel),\displaystyle=\frac{-2.95}{\ln\left(1/2-J_{2}/J_{1}\right)}\;,\;\;\;\;\;\;(\text{N\'{e}el})\;, (31a)
12​S\displaystyle\frac{1}{2S} =2.55​J2/J1−1/2,(stripe).\displaystyle=2.55\sqrt{J_{2}/J_{1}-1/2}\;,\;\;\;\;\;\;(\text{stripe})\;. (31b)

These curves are shown as dashed blue and red lines in Fig. 4, respectively. However, the quantitative picture is rather different from the predictions of spin-wave theory [30] that are for comparison plotted as dash-dotted lines in Fig. 4, with a significantly larger and rather asymmetric paramagnetic region that is wider for J2/J1>0.5J_{2}/J_{1}>0.5 than for J2/J1<0.5J_{2}/J_{1}<0.5. Thus, it appears that the magnitude of frustration-induced quantum fluctuations are overestimated by spin-wave theory for the Néel state and severely underestimated for the stripe state.

IV Summary and outlook

In this work we have studied the zero-temperature phase diagram of the paradigmatic J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} quantum Heisenberg model on a square lattice for arbitrary spin quantum number SS using an advanced implementation [29] of the spin FRG approach proposed in Ref. [22]. Let us summarize the main technical advances reported in this work:

  1. 1.

    The innocent looking spin-length constraint 𝑺i2=S⁡(S+1)\bm{S}_{i}^{2}=S(S+1) implies an infinite tower of sum rules involving vertices of different order which can be elegantly derived using our spin FRG formalism.

  2. 2.

    These sum rules can be used to construct non-perturbative truncations of the formally exact spin FRG flow equations.

  3. 3.

    For frustrated magnets in reduced dimensions the implementation of these sum rules and the constraints imposed by spin conservation and ergodicity are crucial to construct sensible truncations of the spin FRG flow equations.

  4. 4.

    In contrast to the pseudo-fermion FRG approach [14, 15], the implementation of our spin FRG for frustrated magnets does not require heavy numerical calculations; the results presented in this work have been obtained in a few minutes on a desktop computer. It is also not necessary to perform finite-size scaling to detect phase transitions between long-range ordered and paramagnetic phases in the spin FRG, unlike in the pseudo-fermion and pseudo-Majorana FRG implementations. Which method is ultimately preferable for the study of frustrated quantum magnets of course also depends on their respective quantitative accuracy. In this respect, it would be desirable to compare the spin FRG with pseudo-fermion and pseudo-Majorana FRG in benchmark systems where exact results are known by other methods.

  5. 5.

    The spin FRG allows us to investigate quantum spin systems for arbitrary real values of the spin quantum number SS, without additional technical modifications or numerical costs. While implementations of the pseudo-fermion FRG for S>1/2S>1/2 exist [80, 81, 15], they come with additional technical complications because each spin-SS operator is represented by 2​S2S copies of spin-1/21/2 operators, which are then expressed in terms of pseudo-fermions with an additional flavor index. Due to this construction, they are also restricted to integer or half-integer values of SS.

The main physical result obtained in this work is the zero-temperature phase diagram of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model as a function of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and the inverse spin quantum number 1/2​S1/2S shown in Fig. 4. Although spin-wave theory produces a qualitatively similar phase diagram, the shape of the phase boundaries obtained by us is more asymmetric and the extension of the paramagnetic phase significantly larger than predicted by spin-wave theory.

Our approach offers many promising opportunities for further research. The inclusion of an external magnetic field is straightforward and does not add any significant complexity. The door is now wide open to use our spin FRG approach to study ground state properties of more complicated models for frustrated magnets involving other lattices and less symmetric exchange couplings.

APPENDIX A Temperature rescaling

A significant advantage of the multiplicative deformation scheme (4) is that in the absence of external magnetic fields, the temperature dependence can be removed from the problem entirely by rescaling the deformation parameter and Matsubara frequencies as

Λ\displaystyle\Lambda =Λ¯​T,Λ¯∈[0,1/T],\displaystyle=\bar{\Lambda}T\;,\;\;\;\;\;\;\bar{\Lambda}\in[0,1/T]\;, (A1a)
ω\displaystyle\omega =ω¯​T.\displaystyle=\bar{\omega}T\;. (A1b)

It is then straightforward to see from the generating functional (5) that the vertices should be rescaled as

ΓΛα1​…​αn​α~1​…​α~m​(𝒌1,…,𝒌n,(𝒒1,ω1),…,(𝒒m,ωm))=\displaystyle\Gamma_{\Lambda}^{\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{n}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\ldots\tilde{\alpha}_{m}}\left(\bm{k}_{1},\ldots,\bm{k}_{n},(\bm{q}_{1},\omega_{1}),\ldots,(\bm{q}_{m},\omega_{m})\right)= T1−m​Γ¯Λ¯=Λ/Tα1​…​αn​α~1​…​α~m​(𝒌1,…,𝒌n,(𝒒1,ω1/T),…,(𝒒m,ωm/T)),\displaystyle T^{1-m}\bar{\Gamma}_{\bar{\Lambda}=\Lambda/T}^{\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{n}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\ldots\tilde{\alpha}_{m}}\left(\bm{k}_{1},\ldots,\bm{k}_{n},(\bm{q}_{1},\omega_{1}/T),\ldots,(\bm{q}_{m},\omega_{m}/T)\right)\;, (A2a)
Γ¯Λ¯α1​…​αn​α~1​…​α~m​(𝒌1,…,𝒌n,(𝒒1,ω¯1),…,(𝒒m,ω¯m))=\displaystyle\bar{\Gamma}_{\bar{\Lambda}}^{\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{n}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\ldots\tilde{\alpha}_{m}}\left(\bm{k}_{1},\ldots,\bm{k}_{n},(\bm{q}_{1},\bar{\omega}_{1}),\ldots,(\bm{q}_{m},\bar{\omega}_{m})\right)= Tm−1​ΓΛ=Λ¯​Tα1​…​αn​α~1​…​α~m​(𝒌1,…,𝒌n,(𝒒1,ω¯1​T),…,(𝒒m,ω¯m​T)),\displaystyle T^{m-1}\Gamma_{\Lambda=\bar{\Lambda}T}^{\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{n}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\ldots\tilde{\alpha}_{m}}\left(\bm{k}_{1},\ldots,\bm{k}_{n},(\bm{q}_{1},\bar{\omega}_{1}T),\ldots,(\bm{q}_{m},\bar{\omega}_{m}T)\right)\;, (A2b)

where the rescaled Γ¯Λ¯\bar{\Gamma}_{\bar{\Lambda}} vertices do not depend explicitly on the temperature TT. In this way, we obtain an effectively TT-independent problem with T→1T\to 1 at fixed Λ¯\bar{\Lambda}. The TT-dependence is then generated by flowing from Λ¯=0\bar{\Lambda}=0, corresponding to T→∞T\to\infty, to Λ¯=1/T\bar{\Lambda}=1/T. In this form, the only remaining dimensionful quantities are Λ¯\bar{\Lambda} and J⁡(𝒌)J(\bm{k}), which always appear as dimensionless product Λ¯​J​(𝒌)\bar{\Lambda}J(\bm{k}). This rescaling also makes it obvious that by expanding the spin FRG flow equations in powers of Λ¯​J​(𝒌)\bar{\Lambda}J(\bm{k}) we obtain the high-temperature expansion for the spin vertices.

APPENDIX B Spin-length sum rules from spin FRG flow equations

In order to efficiently derive the sum rules associated with the spin-length constraint (15), we write a general deformed Heisenberg Hamiltonian as

ℋΛ\displaystyle{\cal H}_{\Lambda} =12​∑i​jJi​jΛ​𝑺i⋅𝑺j\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}J_{ij}^{\Lambda}\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j} (B3a)
=12​∑i​j[Ji​jΛ+δi​j​CΛ−δi​j​CΛ]​𝑺i⋅𝑺j\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}\left[J_{ij}^{\Lambda}+\delta_{ij}C_{\Lambda}-\delta_{ij}C_{\Lambda}\right]\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j} (B3b)
=12​∑i​j(Ji​jΛ+δi​j​CΛ)​𝑺i⋅𝑺j−N2​CΛ​S​(S+1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}\left(J_{ij}^{\Lambda}+\delta_{ij}C_{\Lambda}\right)\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}-\frac{N}{2}C_{\Lambda}S(S+1)\;, (B3c)

with arbitrary, scale-dependent CΛC_{\Lambda}. This rewriting leads to the following modifications in the flow equations:

  1. (i)

    The constant energy shift adds an additional term

    −12∂ΛCΛS(S+1)-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\Lambda}C_{\Lambda}S(S+1) (B4)

    to the right-hand side of the flow equation of the free energy density fΛf_{\Lambda}.

  2. (ii)

    The on-site shift in the exchange coupling results in the replacement

    ∂ΛJΛ​(𝒒)→∂ΛJΛ​(𝒒)+∂ΛCΛ\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})\to\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{q})+\partial_{\Lambda}C_{\Lambda} (B5)

    everywhere in all flow equations.

  3. (iii)

    The scale-dependent static spin susceptibility is now parametrized as

    GΛ​(𝒌)=1JΛ​(𝒌)+CΛ+Σ~Λ​(𝒌).G_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})=\frac{1}{J_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})+C_{\Lambda}+\tilde{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})}\;. (B6)

The crucial point is now that we did not modify the system at all, but only added a zero to the Hamiltonian regardless of the value of Λ\Lambda. Hence, all correlation functions must remain independent of CΛC_{\Lambda}. Comparing with the original parametrization (7) of the static spin susceptibility, we immediately infer

Σ~Λ​(𝒌)=ΣΛ​(𝒌)−CΛ,\tilde{\Sigma}_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})=\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})-C_{\Lambda}\;, (B7)

where ΣΛ​(𝒌)\Sigma_{\Lambda}(\bm{k}) is independent of CΛC_{\Lambda}. As all other vertex functions in the hybrid functional are defined in terms of spin correlation functions [26], it follows that they must be independent of CΛC_{\Lambda}. Consequently, all ∂ΛCΛ\partial_{\Lambda}C_{\Lambda}-contributions to their flow equations must cancel. For example, the flow of the free energy density is given by

∂ΛfΛ=\displaystyle\partial_{\Lambda}f_{\Lambda}={} 32​∫K[∂ΛJΛ​(𝒌)]​GΛ​(K)​at CΛ=0\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}\int_{K}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})\right]G_{\Lambda}(K)\;\;\;\text{at $C_{\Lambda}=0$} (B8a)
=\displaystyle={} 32​∫K[∂ΛJΛ​(𝒌)+∂ΛCΛ]​GΛ​(K)\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}\int_{K}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})+\partial_{\Lambda}C_{\Lambda}\right]G_{\Lambda}(K)
−12∂ΛCΛS(S+1)\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\Lambda}C_{\Lambda}S(S+1) (B8b)
=\displaystyle={} 32​∫K[∂ΛJΛ​(𝒌)]​GΛ​(K)\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}\int_{K}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}J_{\Lambda}(\bm{k})\right]G_{\Lambda}(K)
+32​[∂ΛCΛ]​[∫KGΛ​(K)−S⁡(S+1)3].\displaystyle+\frac{3}{2}\left[\partial_{\Lambda}C_{\Lambda}\right]\left[\int_{K}G_{\Lambda}(K)-\frac{S(S+1)}{3}\right]\;. (B8c)

Comparing the first and last line of the above yields the susceptibility sum rule (16). This scheme can be applied in the same way to each spin FRG flow equation to yield an associated sum rule for the vertices. In practice, this means that one can apply the rules (i)-(iv) given in Sec. II.2 to any spin FRG flow equation to elegantly derive the associated sum rule, since these rules generate precisely the ∂ΛCΛ\partial_{\Lambda}C_{\Lambda}-contributions that have to vanish in order to guarantee consistency of the correlation functions. Note also that because the hierarchy of spin FRG flow equations is infinite, there is likewise an infinite tower of spin-length sum rules.
